note: The canto opens in the middle of a prayer: the souls of the proud are reciting the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13), which begins "Our Father, who art in heaven". They stretch each petition into three lines, adding words that humble the one who prays.
God is everywhere and nothing contains him. He is said to be in heaven only because that is where his love is most fully received.

quote: the first and highest works of creation
note: The heavens and the angels, the first things God made.
The proud trusted their own powers. Their prayer now admits that no human effort can reach God's peace unless it is given.
A Hebrew cry of praise, shouted by the crowd when Christ rode into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:9).
Dante's Italian says "manna", the food God sent each day to the Israelites in the desert (Exodus 16). Here it means grace, the food of the soul, which fits the "wilderness" of the next line.
The devil.
Souls who have passed the gate of Purgatory can no longer be tempted or sin. They say the prayer's last request, "lead us not into temptation", for the living they left on earth.

The proud carry great stones on their backs, bent so low that their faces are near the ground (Canto 10). The penance fits the sin: those who held their heads above everyone else are bowed to the earth.

context: The lowest of the mountain's seven terraces, where pride is purged. Pride comes first because medieval teaching made it the root of every other sin.

note: The Italian word means mist or soot: the dark film that sin left on the soul, which must be cleaned off before it can see God.
Dante turns to the reader. If the dead pray for the living, the living owe them prayers in return. Throughout Purgatorio, prayers from earth shorten a soul's time on the mountain.

quote: whose will is rooted in goodness
note: Those who live in God's grace. Only their prayers are heard in Heaven, as Belacqua explained in Canto 4.
Virgil speaks, asking the souls the way up. He wins their goodwill first by wishing them a quick release.
Dante's living body, inherited from the first man. It makes the climb hard work for him, as it is not for a shade.
On the mountain the travelers circle to the right, following the sun. In Hell they almost always turned left.

A powerful count of the Maremma, the coastal country of southern Tuscany, and a lifelong enemy of Siena. He died in the 1250s. His son still leads with the great name, then catches himself in the next line.
The Italian says only "the common mother". It is read as the earth, from which all bodies are made, or as Eve. Either way, noble and common people have one origin.

He was killed in 1259 at his castle of Campagnatico, in the war between his family and Siena. Early accounts differ: some say he died fighting Sienese troops, others that hired killers smothered him in his bed.
A hill village in the Ombrone valley, near Grosseto, held by the Aldobrandeschi.

context: The first of three examples of pride in this canto: pride of birth. The other two are pride in one's art (Oderisi) and pride of power (Provenzan Salvani).

note: Dante stoops to hear, and so walks bent over like the proud themselves. Pride is the sin he owns most readily: in Canto 13 he says he already feels the weight of these stones.

context: He knows Dante on sight, and the two speak as fellow artists. His example is pride in one's own skill.

note: Gubbio is a hill town in Umbria, in central Italy. Dante greets him with exactly the kind of praise Oderisi is here to unlearn, and Oderisi at once hands the honor to someone else.

Painting the pages of handwritten books with small pictures, decorated letters and gold. Dante uses a word taken from French rather than the usual Italian one: Paris was the great center of the book trade.
A famous phrase. In Italian the pages "laugh": the bright colors and gold of a painted manuscript.
A manuscript painter of the generation after Oderisi. Nothing survives that is certainly his, which rather proves Oderisi's point about fame.
He repented while he was still alive and able to sin, not on his deathbed. So he was spared the long wait outside the gate that late repenters must serve.
A name stays famous only if a duller age follows, with no one to outdo it. Wherever art keeps improving, each master is soon eclipsed by the next.

context: Dante's contemporary and fellow Florentine. This line is among the earliest written records of his fame.
The younger Guido, who has taken first place in Italian poetry from Guido Guinizzelli.
The older Guido, the poet from Bologna, now overtaken by Cavalcanti. Dante meets him in Canto 26.

note: Almost always read as Dante himself, the poet who will outdo both Guidos. If so, it is a boast made on the terrace of pride, in a speech on the emptiness of fame. Some readers take it as a general remark: someone always comes along.
The Italian has two baby-talk words, "pappo" and "dindi": a small child's words for food and for money.

The sphere of the fixed stars. Besides its daily turn, astronomers gave it a slow drift of one degree in a hundred years, so a full circle took 36,000 years. Against eternity, a thousand years of fame is less than a blink set against that.
The soul just ahead, creeping under his stone. Oderisi names him a few lines on: Provenzan Salvani.
The battle of Montaperti, 1260. Siena and its Ghibelline allies destroyed the army of Guelph Florence, and Florence lost its power for several years. Inferno 10 and 32 return to the same battle.
Dante's Italian is harsher: Florence was proud then and is a whore now, for sale to whoever pays.

An echo of the Bible: "All flesh is grass... the grass withers, the flower fades" (Isaiah 40:6–8). The sun that makes the grass green also dries it out: the same passing of time that brings fame takes it away.
Pride pictured as a tumor. Dante admits it is his own.

context: The third example: pride of power. He died in 1269, only thirty-one years before Dante's journey, which prompts the question that follows.

quote: waits until the edge of life
note: Souls who put off repentance until the end must wait outside the gate of Purgatory for as long as they lived, unless prayers shorten it (Canto 4). Salvani repented late and died recently, so by the rule he should still be down there.

The great sloping square at the center of Siena. Early commentators say a friend of Salvani's was held for a ransom of ten thousand florins, with a deadline, and that the most powerful man in the city sat down in the square and begged passers-by for the money.

context: According to the early commentators, the friend had fought against Charles at Tagliacozzo in 1268 and been taken prisoner.

note: The shame of begging in public, for a proud man. That one act of humility was enough to cancel his waiting time.
A prophecy of Dante's exile. In 1302 his fellow Florentines banished him, and he spent the rest of his life dependent on the hospitality of others. He will learn for himself what it costs to ask.
The slopes below the gate, where the late repenters wait.
